cards.explanation: The answer is True. Peter says, "But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed." (1 Peter 3:14) Suffering and blessing in the same sentence is a lot to chew on, friends, but that's what the text says. And Peter wrote it to people he calls "exiles" (1 Peter 1:1).

The answer is in their hearts. Peter says, "But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord." (1 Peter 3:15) No building needed, no special address. This one happens right where you are, on the inside, even on a day when everything outside is rattling.

The answer is the reason for the hope in them. Peter says to be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks "…the reason for the hope that is in you." (1 Peter 3:15) Notice it's about hope, friends. Nobody has to win a debate, just be ready to say why they have it.

The answer is True. Peter says, "But respond with gentleness and respect…" (1 Peter 3:15) So the answer matters, and so does how it's delivered. I think a soft voice can carry a hard truth a lot farther than a loud one.

The answer is that it puts them to shame. Peter says those who slander the believers "…may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ." (1 Peter 3:16) Good behavior speaks up without raising its voice. I think that's a quiet kind of comeback.

The answer is False. Peter writes, "For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil." (1 Peter 3:17) Suffering for doing good is the better of the two. Peter wants the believers to keep doing good.

The answer is once for all. Peter says, "For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." (1 Peter 3:18) Once. Not a repeat, not a second round. One time, and Peter says it was for the unrighteous.

The answer is True. Peter says Christ suffered "…the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." (1 Peter 3:18) That's the purpose in the text, friends. He did it to bring the believers to God.
The answer is False. Peter says, "He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit…" (1 Peter 3:18) He didn't stay dead. Peter says He was made alive.

The answer is in the days of Noah. Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) Noah is the man God told to build the ark (Genesis 6:14). God's patience is right there in the text.

The answer is water. Peter says, "In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water." (1 Peter 3:20) Eight souls, and the water is part of how they were saved. A small number in a big story.

The answer is baptism. Peter says, "And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also…" (1 Peter 3:21) He ties Noah's water to the believers' own day, friends. The word he uses is baptism.

The answer is False. Peter says baptism is "…not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) It isn't about dirt on the body. Peter points to the conscience instead.

The answer is a pledge of a clear conscience toward God. Peter calls it "…the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) It's about the conscience, not about dirt. And he says it saves "…through the resurrection of Jesus Christ…"

The answer is that they are subject to Him. Peter says Jesus "…has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him." (1 Peter 3:22) Angels, authorities and powers are all subject to Him. That's a good place to end the passage.
